author: A Robot
objectives: Students will identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Students will trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order.
Students will distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions.

Students will explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to the pressure required to perfuse the systemic versus pulmonary circuits.
Students will describe the function of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves in preventing backflow, and identify which valves separate which chambers or chamber-vessel pairs.

modules.description: Students examine a three-dimensional model of the human heart, identify its four chambers, and explore the major vessels connecting to it.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify and name the four chambers of the heart: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, and left ventricle.
Locate the major vessels entering and leaving the heart, including the superior and inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries and veins, and the aorta.
Recognize the external appearance and relative position of each chamber on the heart surface.
instructions: A 3-D heart model will appear on your table. Use Next and Previous to step through the narrated tour.
Labels will highlight each structure as it is introduced. Take a moment to view each from multiple angles.
Pay attention to the color-coded chambers — blue for right-side structures (deoxygenated) and red for left-side structures (oxygenated).

components.text: Human Heart — External Anatomy

Right Atrium
Receives deoxygenated blood from the body

Right Ventricle
Pumps blood to the lungs (pulmonary circuit)

Left Atrium
Receives oxygenated blood from the lungs

Left Ventricle
Pumps blood to the entire body (systemic circuit)

Superior & Inferior Vena Cava
Return deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium

Aorta
Largest artery; carries oxygenated blood to the systemic circuit

Pulmonary Arteries & Veins
Connect the heart to the lungs for gas exchange

clips.changeMeaning: The heart model appears centered on the table, slowly rotating so students can appreciate its three-dimensional form from all angles. The title label is visible above it.
clips.narration: Welcome to the Human Heart AR Lab. Here you can see a three-dimensional model of the human heart rendered at roughly 60% of life size. The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump sitting in the mediastinum of the thoracic cavity. Over the next several scenes you will explore its chambers, valves, major vessels, and the dual circulatory loops it drives. Let's begin by orienting ourselves to the external anatomy.

clips.changeMeaning: Labels for the right atrium, right ventricle, and the vena cavae appear, and the heart model is tinted blue on its right side to reinforce the color-coding convention for deoxygenated blood.
clips.narration: The right side of the heart is shown here in blue, indicating that it handles deoxygenated blood. The right atrium is the upper-right chamber. It receives blood returning from the body through the superior vena cava, which drains the head and upper limbs, and the inferior vena cava, which drains the lower body. Just below the right atrium sits the right ventricle, which pumps that deoxygenated blood toward the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Labels for the left atrium and left ventricle appear. The heart model color shifts to red on its left side, visually distinguishing oxygenated from deoxygenated sides.
clips.narration: Now let's look at the left side, shown in red, which handles oxygenated blood returning from the lungs. The left atrium, the upper-left chamber, receives blood from the four pulmonary veins. Below it, the left ventricle is the most muscular chamber of all — it must generate enough pressure to push blood through the entire systemic circulation, all the way to your toes and back.

clips.changeMeaning: Labels for the aorta and pulmonary vessels appear, completing the full external anatomy labeling. The heart model returns to its natural texture color so students can cross-reference with an anatomical view.
clips.narration: The major vessels connecting to the heart complete the picture. Superiorly, the aorta arches upward from the left ventricle — this is the largest artery in the body. The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle and splits into the left and right pulmonary arteries, carrying blood to each lung. Four pulmonary veins, two from each lung, return oxygenated blood to the left atrium. Together these vessels form the two great circuits of the cardiovascular system.

modules.description: Students examine the four heart valves in cross-section, learning their locations, structural types, and roles in preventing backflow during the cardiac cycle.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Name and locate all four heart valves: tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral (bicuspid), and aortic.
Distinguish atrioventricular (AV) valves from semilunar valves and describe their structural differences.
Explain how valve opening and closing prevents backflow of blood during systole and diastole.
instructions: A cross-sectional view of the heart will be shown highlighting each valve in turn.
Look for the number of cusps (leaflets) on each valve — this is how they get their names.
Focus on which structures each valve separates: chamber-to-chamber or chamber-to-vessel.

components.text: Heart Valves — Cross-Section View

Tricuspid Valve (AV)
3 cusps | Right atrium → Right ventricle
Prevents backflow during ventricular contraction

Pulmonary Valve (Semilunar)
3 half-moon cusps | Right ventricle → Pulmonary trunk
Prevents backflow from pulmonary artery

Mitral Valve / Bicuspid (AV)
2 cusps | Left atrium → Left ventricle
Prevents backflow during ventricular contraction

Aortic Valve (Semilunar)
3 half-moon cusps | Left ventricle → Aorta
Prevents backflow from aorta
AV Valves open during diastole (ventricular filling) | Semilunar Valves open during systole (ventricular ejection)

clips.changeMeaning: The cross-section model of the heart appears on the table, showing all four chambers in a frontal cut. The title label orients the student to the new view.
clips.narration: We are now looking at a frontal cross-section of the heart. This view cuts through all four chambers and exposes the four valves that control blood flow. There are two types of valves: the atrioventricular, or AV, valves between the atria and ventricles, and the semilunar valves between the ventricles and the great vessels. Let's look at each one.

clips.changeMeaning: The tricuspid valve highlight glows blue on the cross-section model and its detailed label appears to the right, drawing the student's attention to the right AV junction.
clips.narration: On the right side, between the right atrium and right ventricle, sits the tricuspid valve — named for its three cusps, or leaflets. It is an atrioventricular valve, meaning it lies between an atrium and a ventricle. When the right ventricle contracts, pressure closes the tricuspid valve, preventing blood from surging back into the right atrium. Chordae tendineae, tiny fibrous cords attached to papillary muscles, anchor the leaflets so they don't prolapse upward.

clips.changeMeaning: The pulmonary valve highlight activates and its label appears, showing students the right ventricular outflow tract and the semilunar valve position above the tricuspid.
clips.narration: Moving superiorly on the right side, where the pulmonary trunk exits the right ventricle, we find the pulmonary valve — a semilunar valve with three half-moon-shaped cusps. During ventricular systole, when the right ventricle contracts, this valve is pushed open and blood flows into the pulmonary trunk toward the lungs. When systole ends and pressure in the right ventricle drops, the cusps snap shut, preventing pulmonary arterial blood from flowing back into the ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: The mitral valve highlight glows red and its label appears on the left side, contrasting with the tricuspid and reinforcing the structural symmetry between the two AV valves.
clips.narration: On the left side, between the left atrium and left ventricle, is the mitral valve, also called the bicuspid valve because it has only two cusps. It is the left-sided atrioventricular valve. Like the tricuspid, it is anchored by chordae tendineae. When the left ventricle contracts, the mitral valve snaps shut to prevent blood from flowing back up into the left atrium. Mitral valve prolapse and stenosis are among the most clinically common valve disorders.

clips.changeMeaning: The aortic valve highlight activates and its label appears. All four valve highlights and labels are now visible simultaneously, giving students the complete four-valve overview before the summary clip.
clips.narration: Finally, at the root of the aorta where it exits the left ventricle, is the aortic valve — another semilunar valve with three cusps. This valve must withstand the highest pressures in the heart, since the left ventricle generates roughly 120 millimeters of mercury during systole. When the left ventricle relaxes, the aortic valve closes, and the sinuses of Valsalva behind each cusp help prevent the cusps from sticking to the aortic wall, ensuring reliable closure with every beat.

clips.changeMeaning: A summary label appears at the bottom of the scene consolidating the AV vs. semilunar valve functional distinction. All highlights remain visible so students can cross-reference the summary text with the model.
clips.narration: Let's summarize. The two AV valves — tricuspid on the right, mitral on the left — open during ventricular diastole, allowing the ventricles to fill with blood from the atria. They close at the onset of ventricular systole. The two semilunar valves — pulmonary on the right, aortic on the left — open during ventricular systole as the ventricles eject blood, then close during diastole to prevent backflow from the great vessels. This elegant, passive mechanism driven by pressure gradients ensures unidirectional blood flow through the heart with every single beat.

modules.moduleName: Blood Flow Through the Dual Circulation
modules.description: Students trace the complete path of blood through both the pulmonary and systemic circuits, following animated blood-drop markers through each chamber, valve, and vessel in sequence.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace deoxygenated blood from the vena cavae through the right heart and pulmonary circuit to the lungs.
Trace oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins through the left heart and into the systemic aorta.
Explain why the left ventricle wall is substantially thicker than the right ventricle wall.
instructions: Animated blood-drop markers will travel through the heart model, showing the path of blood step by step.
Blue markers represent deoxygenated blood; red markers represent oxygenated blood.
A route label will update at each step — read it carefully before advancing.

components.text: Blood Flow Through the Heart
Dual Circulation — Pulmonary & Systemic Circuits

Left Ventricle wall is ~3× thicker than Right Ventricle wall.
Reason: must generate ~5× higher pressure to perfuse systemic circulation.

clips.changeMeaning: The heart flow model appears. The title and circuit-type label set context for the dual-loop concept. No blood drops are shown yet, building anticipation.
clips.narration: In this scene we will trace the complete journey of blood through the heart. The heart drives two separate but connected loops: the pulmonary circuit, which sends blood to the lungs for oxygenation, and the systemic circuit, which delivers oxygenated blood to every organ and tissue in the body. We will follow both a blue deoxygenated blood drop and a red oxygenated blood drop through the entire sequence.

components.text: Step 1 → Deoxygenated blood enters the RIGHT ATRIUM via Superior & Inferior Vena Cava

clips.changeMeaning: The blue deoxygenated blood drop appears at the superior vena cava entry point near the right atrium and moves downward to sit inside the right atrium. The flow step label updates to indicate step 1.
clips.narration: Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium via the superior vena cava, draining the head, neck, and upper limbs, and the inferior vena cava, draining the abdomen and lower limbs. The coronary sinus also empties venous blood from the heart muscle itself into the right atrium. The right atrium acts as a receiving chamber, allowing pressure to build before the tricuspid valve opens.

components.text: Step 2 → Through TRICUSPID VALVE into RIGHT VENTRICLE → Through PULMONARY VALVE into Pulmonary Trunk

clips.changeMeaning: The blue blood drop moves inferiorly into the right ventricle position, then arcs upward toward the pulmonary outflow tract, animating the passage through the tricuspid and then pulmonary valve. The flow label updates.
clips.narration: When the right atrium contracts and ventricular pressure drops during diastole, the tricuspid valve opens and blood flows down into the right ventricle. The right ventricle then contracts — this is ventricular systole — snapping the tricuspid valve shut and forcing blood upward and out through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk, which quickly branches into the left and right pulmonary arteries heading to each lung.

components.text: Step 3 → Pulmonary arteries → LUNGS (gas exchange) → Oxygenated blood returns via Pulmonary Veins to LEFT ATRIUM

clips.changeMeaning: The lungs model appears behind the heart. The blue blood drop travels to the lungs model and transforms to red, showing oxygenation. The red blood drop then appears at the left atrium. The flow label updates to describe the pulmonary circuit.
clips.narration: The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the capillary beds surrounding the alveoli of the lungs. Here, carbon dioxide diffuses out of the blood and oxygen diffuses in — this is external respiration. The now-oxygenated blood collects into the pulmonary veins. Uniquely, these are the only veins in the body that carry oxygenated blood. Four pulmonary veins — two from each lung — drain back into the left atrium.

components.text: Step 4 → Through MITRAL VALVE into LEFT VENTRICLE → Through AORTIC VALVE into AORTA → Systemic Circulation

clips.changeMeaning: The red blood drop moves into the left ventricle then arcs out toward the aorta position. The flow label updates to complete the systemic circuit pathway, giving students the full sequence from left atrium through the aorta.
clips.narration: Oxygenated blood now fills the left atrium. When the left atrium contracts and the mitral valve opens, blood flows into the left ventricle. The left ventricle is the powerhouse of the heart. It contracts vigorously during systole, closing the mitral valve and forcing blood through the aortic valve into the aorta at a peak pressure of about 120 millimeters of mercury. From the aorta, oxygenated blood is distributed to the brain, organs, muscles, and every cell in the body before returning deoxygenated to the right atrium, completing the cycle.

components.text: Left Ventricle: ~120 mmHg (systemic) vs. Right Ventricle: ~25 mmHg (pulmonary) — pressure drives wall thickness!

clips.changeMeaning: The wall thickness comparison label appears at the front of the scene. The heart model subtly highlights the left ventricular wall in a warmer color to draw attention to the thickness difference, reinforcing the physiological explanation.
clips.narration: Notice the difference in wall thickness between the left and right ventricles. The right ventricle needs only modest pressure — roughly 25 millimeters of mercury — to push blood through the low-resistance pulmonary circuit to the nearby lungs. The left ventricle, however, must overcome the far greater resistance of the entire systemic circulation, generating pressures around 120 millimeters of mercury. This demand is reflected in the myocardium: the left ventricular wall is approximately three times thicker than the right. You can see this asymmetry clearly in the cross-section before you.
